newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BSE epidemic almost didn't happen, Commission official says.
newsitem.headline: BSE epidemic almost didn't happen, Commission official says.

text.p: The mad cow epidemic almost didn't happen, a European Commission official told a European Parliament committee of inquiry on Monday.
"This was an outbreak which nearly did not happen," Brian Marchant, the official responsible for Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) in the Commission's agricultural directorate said.
He was defending action taken by the Commission to prevent the spread of mad cow disease which is believed to be caused by infected meat and bone meal added to cattle feed.
In March, the Commission banned exports of British beef after London admitted a link between BSE and a new form of a similar human brain disorder, Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease (CJD).
Marchant defended a decision to process gelatine at 133 degrees centigrade for 20 minutes in order to deactivate the BSE agent.

"The 133 degree rule does give a very high degree of protection but if there is a very high level of infectivity in the material (being used) it may not be adequate to deactivate the agent," he told the MEPs.
High levels of material from sheep infected with scrapie had overwhelmed the system of heat treatment designed to deactivate BSE and other infectious agents.
Marchant described attacks on the Commission by MEPs as 'vitriolic' and said there was no evidence that controls introduced by the Commission to control BSE were inadequate.
The Commisison had been misled by European gelatine manufacturers into a conditional relaxation of a ban on British gelatine, he said.
"I think we (the Commission) were fooled, deliberately or otherwise," he told the inquiry.
The gelatine manufacturers submitted a contradictory final report calling for more research into the health risk after the Commission had acted on the findings of an interim report.
